abstract.text: Injury-related pain and anxiety are common among children in the emergency department (ED) and often inadequately treated despite existing guidelines. This study aimed to assess the proportion of children who received adequate pain and anxiety relief in a Danish ED.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective study of 184 children (0-17 years) presenting with injuries at a level 1 trauma centre in Denmark (September-October 2025). Pain and anxiety were assessed during observation in the clinic using the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) Scale (≤ 5 years) and the Wong-Baker visual analogue scale (VAS) (> 5 years). Adequate relief was defined as a FLACC Scale score ≤ 3 or a Wong-Baker VAS in the 1-3 range. We collected data on treatments, non-pharmacological interventions, senior anaesthesiologist involvement, satisfaction and adverse effects during the visit and through follow-up calls.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In the study, 50% (92 children, 95% CI: 43-57%) received adequate pain and anxiety relief. Non-pharmacological interventions were rarely used (not used in 57% of children ≤ 5 years and in 97% of children > 5 years). Although a senior paediatric anaesthesiologist was always available for phone consultation, this was used in only 1.7% of cases (n = 3). Adverse effects of medication were observed in 16.2% of children during the ED visit (6/37 treated with medications).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Half of paediatric patients did not receive adequate pain and/or anxiety relief in the ED. Protocolled non-pharmacological strategies and consultations with the available senior anaesthesiologist were rarely used.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: None.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Not relevant.

articles.title: Traffic injuries after orthopaedic surgery.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Orthopaedic surgery and post-operative immobilisation can impair the ability to remain safe in traffic and potentially increase the risk of traffic-related incidents. The aim of this study was to assess the incidence of traffic-related injuries during the first year after orthopaedic surgery.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cohort study included patients who underwent orthopaedic surgery at Odense University Hospitals, Denmark, from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2024 with a 12-month follow-up. Traffic-related injuries were identified from emergency department records. Descriptive statistics summarised patient characteristics, surgical types, and outcomes. We analysed time to traffic incident and mode of transportation to assess temporal patterns.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 17,526 orthopaedic patients were included; 53.7% were women. Only 117 patients (0.7%), 55.6% male, were treated for traffic-related injuries. The proportion of traffic-related injuries was highest among younger patients, with 2.3% aged 18-24 years. Most injuries involved cyclists (44.4%), followed by motorised transport (30.8%), and were mainly solo incidents (60.7%). No clear clustering by transportation mode was observed. Fewer incidents occurred in the early post-operative period, with a gradual increase being observed over time.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Within the first year after surgery, 0.7% experienced a traffic incident requiring emergency department contact. This proportion appeared comparable to the background rate of traffic-related emergency department contacts in Denmark.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: None.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Not relevant.

articles.title: Impact of Physician Patient Load on Imaging Use in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) crowding may alter physician decision-making, yet little is known about how real-time physician workload affects diagnostic imaging use. We examined the association between physician patient load and the proportion of patients who received diagnostic imaging, including computed tomography (CT), CT with intravenous (IV) contrast, CT without contrast, plain radiography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound (US).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of all ED visits at an academic tertiary care center (January 2019-December 2024). Physician workload was defined as the sequential patient assignment order per physician per day (range 1-17). Our primary outcome measures were binary indicators of whether each imaging modality was ordered during the ED visit: CT (any); CT with IV contrast; CT without IV contrast; radiograph, MRI; and US. Multivariable logistic regression with physician-clustered robust standard errors estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for each imaging modality, controlling for age, sex, triage acuity, chief complaint, and temporal factors. We also performed mixed-effects logistic regression with physician random intercepts and a within-between (Mundlak) decomposition. Absolute risk differences (ARD) were computed for the 17th versus the first patient.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 287,925 encounters across approximately 41,132 physician shifts managed by 77 physicians, higher workload was associated with decreased odds of imaging for most modalities. Computed tomography with IV contrast showed the strongest effect (aOR 0.990, 95% CI, 0.986-0.994; within-physician aOR 0.991; ARD -2.2 percentage points [pp], from 21.8% to 19.6%). Results were as follows: any CT, aOR 0.994 (0.991-0.997); ARD -1.9 pp (from 38.7% to 36.8%); radiograph, aOR 0.994 (0.990-0.998, P < .001); ARD -1.6 pp (from 44.2% to 42.6%); US, aOR 0.994 (0.990-0.998, P < .001); ARD -0.7 pp (from 9.9% to 9.2%); and MRI was nonsignificant in the pooled model (aOR 0.993, P = .09) but significant in the mixed-effects model (P < .001). Noncontrast CT was unaffected (aOR 1.000, P = .87). Intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.020-0.047, indicating 2-5% of imaging variance was attributable to physician-level differences.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Higher physician workload was associated with modestly reduced imaging use, particularly for resource-intensive modalities. Noncontrast CT was unaffected. Within-physician analyses were consistent with the interpretation that these effects reflect real-time behavioral adaptation rather than physician practice style alone. These findings highlight a trade-off between throughput and diagnostic testing that warrants further study of its impact on clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Patient vs. Companion Satisfaction in the Emergency Department: Cross-sectional, Telephone-Based Survey.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: In Lebanon, it is common for multiple family members to accompany patients to the ED. In this cultural context, where family is closely involved with patient care, we sought to identify and compare factors associated with satisfaction among patients and their companions during the same emergency department (ED) visit.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional, telephone-based survey compared factors associated with satisfaction among adult patients and their companions, during the same ED visit, at a tertiary-care center in Beirut, Lebanon. Adult patients presenting to the ED with intermediate- or low-acuity complaints were included in the study. We administered a questionnaire to patients and their companions covering six domains, including demographics, general admission, nursing and medical teams, discharge process, and overall satisfaction. Satisfaction was then categorized into high and low. We conducted an analysis of variables associated with high overall satisfaction for each group.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 100 patients and 100 companions completed the survey, with a 45.7% response rate. Among companions, the top three factors associated with high overall satisfaction were: respect of confidentiality and privacy (odds ratio 12.98, 95% CI, 4.79-35.19), length of stay before being seen by triage nurse (9.77, 3.68-25.89), and overall ED length of stay (9.56, 3.7-24.37). Among patients, the top three factors associated with high overall satisfaction were: amount of time the physician spent with the patient (20.26, 7.10-57.82); overall ED length of stay (19.71, 5.44-71.39), and length of stay before being seen by the emergency physician team (13.26, 4.84-36.35). All variables were statistically significant for both patients and companions except for the discharge process, which was only significant for companions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study suggests that patients and companions may have different experiences of their ED visit, highlighting the top factors associated with satisfaction for each group. Emergency department efforts aimed at enhancing patient experience should also consider processes related to companion experience in cultural contexts where family/relatives play an integral role in patient care.

articles.title: Syphilis Screening in Pregnancy During Emergency Department Gonorrhea and Chlamydia Testing.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Congenital syphilis is rising in the United States, especially among infants born to women with limited prenatal care. Emergency departments (ED) offer opportunities for early detection, particularly among patients evaluated for urogenital sexually transmitted infection (STI) concerns. In October 2019, our health system implemented an ED STI order set that promoted HIV co-testing and included a preselected option for syphilis testing. In this study, we evaluated change in syphilis testing during the post-implementation period among ED encounters with both pregnancy and gonorrhea/chlamydia (GC/CT) testing.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective, quasi-experimental study across 20 EDs, using health record data from 2018 to 2023 for patients aged 15-44 years who received both pregnancy and GC/CT testing. We measured annual syphilis and HIV testing and positivity, stratified by pregnancy status. The primary study outcome was syphilis testing during the encounter; HIV testing and detection outcomes were secondary.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 59,171 ED encounters with pregnancy and GC/CT testing, 5,178 (8.8%) involved pregnant patients, and 9,538 (16.1%) received syphilis testing. Syphilis testing among pregnant patients increased from .9% in 2018 to 46.1% in 2023 (+45.1 percentage points [95% CI, 40.4-49.6]). Testing among nonpregnant patients rose from 1.2% to 35.9% (+34.6 percentage points [95% CI, 33.3-35.9]). Overall, only 1,068 of 5,178 pregnant encounters received a syphilis test (20.6%). Among 1,068 syphilis-tested pregnant encounters, 15 (1.4%) were treponemal-positive and 9 (.8%; 843 per 100,000 tested) met the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance definition for active syphilis (approximately 1 per 119 tests). Using all pregnant encounters with GC/CT testing as the denominator, the encounter-based active syphilis rate was 173.8 per 100,000 (.17%). HIV testing increased similarly (pregnant: .4% in 2018 to 44.5% in 2023), while HIV positivity remained rare (2 pregnant; 13 overall).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Syphilis testing and case detection increased during the postimplementation period following introduction of a preselected STI order set in the electronic health record. Many encounters in the analytic cohort still did not include syphilis testing. These findings support the ED as an important setting for identifying syphilis in pregnancy while underscoring the need for further work to understand remaining testing gaps.

articles.title: Impact of Secure Electronic Health Record Chat on Physician Communication in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Effective communication in the emergency department (ED) is essential for safe patient care. Electronic health record (EHR)-integrated secure messaging may improve communication workflows, but limited evidence exists comparing clinician satisfaction across modalities in the ED. This study evaluated physician satisfaction with an EHR-integrated secure messaging tool compared to existing communication methods for non-emergent communication.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted an electronic pre-post survey study at an urban academic ED following implementation of an EHR-integrated secure messaging tool in October 2024. The primary outcome was overall communication satisfaction pre-post implementation. We also compared nursing communication satisfaction and repeat consult order proportions. Survey domains (ease of use, efficiency, timeliness, clarity, overall satisfaction) were graded using a four-point forced-choice Likert scale.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Response rates were 35% (33/95) pre-implementation and 36% (34/95) post-implementation. Although face-to-face communication maintained superior clarity ratings, secure chat received significantly higher overall satisfaction than phone communication (median 3 [IQR 3-4] vs 2 [2-3], P < .001) and higher ratings than the existing consult workflow across all domains (all P ≤ .03). Overall nursing communication satisfaction shifted toward higher scores post-implementation (median 3 [3-4] vs 3 [2-3], P = .03). Repeat consult order proportion decreased from 22% to 18% (risk difference, -3.5%; 95% CI, -4.5% to -2.5%; P < .001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Electronic health record-integrated secure messaging demonstrated high user satisfaction among emergency physicians and may reduce repeat consultant communications. Secure chat provides a complementary communication channel in the ED setting.

articles.title: Higher Intensity Quality Improvement Campaign Yields Greater Reduction in Medical Glove Use: The "Gloves Off!" Campaign.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The healthcare sector contributes 5.4-7.0% of Australia's total carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. Among the most ubiquitous items used in healthcare organisations, whether it be hospital, clinic, or community health centres, are gloves.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We reviewed two case studies of the "Gloves Off!" sustainability initiative to compare reduction in glove use and improvement in hand hygiene practice-one that featured a "low-intensity" campaign (Hospital A) and the other a "high-intensity" campaign (Hospital B).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A comparison of glove use over the year before and after implementation of the Gloves Off! campaign shows that Hospital A achieved a 2.6% reduction (0.4% reduction per patient), while Hospital B achieved an 11.4% reduction in total glove consumption (7.8% reduction in glove use per patient).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Sustainability initiatives can be initiated within busy emergency departments with reduced unnecessary use of nonsterile gloves, decreased CO2 emissions, and cost savings.

articles.title: Standardized Exam of the Abdomen Protocol Through Telemedicine in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Abdominal pain is a common emergency department (ED) presentation, and virtual assessment of such complaints remains a challenge due to the limitations of remote physical examination. The standardized exam of the abdomen protocol (SEAP) was developed to guide patients in performing a self-abdominal examination during telemedicine consultations. We aimed to evaluate agreement between patient-performed abdominal self-examinations using the SEAP and physician-performed abdominal examinations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective, single-center study at the American University of Beirut Medical Center ED in Lebanon from August 2023-August 2024. Adult patients who presented with abdominal pain and met the inclusion criteria were enrolled. Each patient performed a video-guided abdominal self-examination by following a brief instructional video (SEAP). The SEAP was developed by an emergency medicine faculty at our institution using pre-established abdominal examination principles and clinical practice frameworks. The protocol was translated into a structured, two-minute instructional video. Blinded abdominal examinations were then performed by an emergency medicine resident and an attending physician. The primary outcome was agreement in abdominal tenderness across seven predefined regions, assessed using the Cohen kappa coefficient. Patient experience and feasibility measures were also collected.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included a total of 103 patients. Agreement between patient-performed and physician-performed examinations was slight to fair across six of the seven abdominal regions (κ range, .13-.41). The highest agreement was observed in the right lower quadrant, with fair agreement between patients and residents (κ = .47; 95% CI, 0.30-0.64) and patients and attending physicians (κ = .36; 95% CI, 0.18-0.53). Agreement in the remaining regions, including the upper quadrants and flanks, remained low; right upper quadrant (κ = .13), left upper quadrant (κ = .28), and flanks (κ range, -0.04 to .41). Most patients (97.9%; n = 94/96) rated the instructional video as clear and easy to follow.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Patient-performed abdominal self-examination using the SEAP demonstrated limited agreement with physician examinations across most abdominal regions. Agreement in the right lower quadrant was also fair. These findings indicate that patient-performed abdominal self-examination does not reliably reproduce physician assessment. However, they provide a foundation for further studies aimed at refining and better defining the role of patient-guided abdominal examinations in telemedicine settings.

articles.title: Resident Exposure to Acutely Ill Patients Over the Course of Residency.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency medicine literature has long debated the "black cloud" and "white cloud" phenomena, which suggest individual variability in exposure to acutely ill patients. If true, this variation may have significant implications for resident training. This study investigates whether emergency medicine (EM) residents consistently encounter differing volumes of high-acuity clinical encounters throughout their training.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study analyzed 11 years of electronic health record (HER) data from a Midwestern academic emergency department to quantify the number of acutely ill adult patients seen by EM residents across three years of training, using a consensus-based set of clinical criteria. Our primary outcome was the concordance of the ranking of each resident within their cohort by number of acutely ill patients seen during postgraduate year one (PGY 1) compared to PGY 3. Statistical analyses to assess this outcome included weighted kappa and linear regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 93 EM residents met the criteria for inclusion and saw a total of 359,736 patients during their residency (average 3,493 per resident). Residents saw an average of 167.5 (19.8) acutely ill patients during their residency training. This volume increased sharply by year, with PGY-1 residents seeing an average of 23.8 (7.3) acutely ill patients, and PGY-3 residents seeing an average of 100.3 (19.4). Both weighted kappa (κ = -.274) and linear regression analysis (β = -0.84; 95% CI, -1.4 to -0.31; P = .002) indicated that a resident who saw more acutely ill patients than average in PGY 1 was more likely to see fewer acutely ill patients than average during PGY 3. Results were unaffected by the COVID-19 years or subsequent critical care fellowship pursuit.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: "Cloud type" (as measured by EHR-documented care for acutely ill patients) does not appear to be a stable trait over time. Our findings are consistent with previous studies that found no association between residents' "cloudiness" and objective measures of workload. Using EHR data to track resident clinical exposures helps educators identify training gaps and target remediation through in situ or simulated experiences.

articles.title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound After Medical Screening Exam Reduces Time to Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Diagnosis and Surgery.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Ectopic pregnancy remains the leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality. Delays in diagnosis and operative management increase morbidity and may be exacerbated by emergency department (ED) crowding. We evaluated whether integration of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) into the medical screening exam of pregnant patients-the obstetric medical screening exam-was associated with improved timeliness of care for patients with surgically managed ectopic pregnancy.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing operative management for ruptured ectopic pregnancy between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2023, at a county safety-net hospital. The obstetric screening exam was implemented July 12, 2021, and incorporated focused transabdominal pelvic and right upper quadrant ultrasound into the initial ED evaluation, often prior to bed assignment. The primary outcome was time from ED arrival to operating room (OR). Secondary outcomes included time to obstetric consultation, time to hospital admission, ED length of stay (LOS), and POCUS use. Nonparametric testing was used for skewed time data. Logistic regression evaluated the odds of reaching the OR within four hours. Patient-level interrupted time series analysis assessed temporal trends.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 150 patients were included (87 pre- and 63 post-implementation). Median arrival-to-OR time decreased from 516 minutes (interquartile range [IQR] 324-709.5) to 391 minutes (IQR 220-619), a 125-minute reduction (P = .020; bootstrap 95% CI, 8-233). The proportion of patients reaching the OR within four hours increased from 16.1% to 31.8% (odds ratio 2.42; 95% CI, 1.11-5.29; P = .02). Time to obstetric consultation (210 vs 146 minutes; P = .003), time to hospital admission (345 vs 250 minutes; P = .005), and ED LOS (451 vs 367 minutes; P = .03) were all reduced. Point-of-care ultrasound use increased from 41.4% to 66.7% (P < .001), while the remainder underwent radiology ultrasound. Interrupted time series analysis demonstrated no significant immediate change after implementation (P = .790), but a significant postintervention trend toward reduced arrival-to-OR time (-0.45 minutes/day, P = .01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Embedding POCUS into the medical screening examination in triage was associated with sustained improvement in operative timeliness for ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Early diagnostic integration within ED workflow may mitigate system-level delays in time-sensitive obstetric emergencies.

articles.title: Acute Headache Management and Emergency Department Throughput: A Multicenter Retrospective Analysis.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Headache is a common presentation to the emergency department (ED), requiring both accurate diagnosis and efficient management. Although consensus guidelines exist, real-world treatment practices and their associations with operational outcomes remain variable. We evaluated the association between acute headache management strategies-including medications, diagnostic imaging, and consultations-and ED length of stay (LOS), using both unadjusted and multivariable-adjusted analyses.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a multicenter retrospective observational study using data from 79,527 adult ED encounters for headache across 22 EDs in the southwestern and upper Midwestern United States between 2018 and 2024. The primary outcome was ED LOS. Secondary outcomes included LOS differences associated with medication classes, imaging modalities, procedures, and specialty consultations. Length of stay differences by treatment strategy were compared using Mann-Whitney U testing. We performed multivariable linear regression and quantile regression (median) adjusting for age, sex, Emergency Severity Index level, disposition, imaging, procedures, consultations, site, and year. Encounters were classified by headache type (primary, secondary, or unspecified) using discharge diagnosis codes, and stratified analyses were performed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Primary headache encounters comprised 19.4% of the cohort (n = 15,413), secondary headache 14.0% (n = 11,147), and unspecified headache 66.6% (n = 52,967). The overall median LOS was 183 minutes (interquartile range [IQR], 119-276). In unadjusted analyses, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (median 180 vs 185 minutes; P = .42) and triptan administration (177 vs 183 minutes; P = .49) were not associated with longer LOS. In contrast, antiseizure medications (+136 minutes; P < .001), intravenous magnesium (+101 minutes; P < .001), opioids (+89 minutes; P < .001), and benzodiazepines (+72 minutes; P < .001) were associated with the longest LOS. In multivariable-adjusted analysis (R2 = .40), antiseizure medications (adjusted coefficient +85.1 min; 95% CI, 76.0-94.3), admission (+71.1 minutes; 95% CI, 68.3-73.8), and magnetic resonance imaging (+125.9 minutes; 95% CI, 119.8-131.9) were most strongly associated with longer LOS. Stratified analyses showed primary headaches had shorter median LOS (153 minutes; IQR, 105-224) than secondary (204 minutes; IQR, 126-317) or unspecified headaches (189 minutes; IQR, 123-282), with consistent medication-LOS associations across subgroups (Kruskal-Wallis H = 1,476.85, P < .001; all pairwise comparisons P < .001 after Bonferroni correction).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this multicenter retrospective study, most pharmacologic and diagnostic interventions-aside from NSAIDs and triptans-were associated with longer ED LOS, even after adjusting for patient and clinical covariates. These associations likely reflect both direct treatment effects and confounding by indication. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate whether standardized protocols can improve ED throughput while maintaining care quality.

articles.title: Introducing the Climate Change Special Issue.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

articles.title: Reevaluating the Role and Timing of Fever in Acute Cholecystitis.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute cholecystitis is diagnosed based on clinical and diagnostic findings. Fever is commonly considered a sign of systemic inflammation in acute cholecystitis, although its diagnostic performance may vary depending on the timing of presentation. This study analyzed the prevalence of fever as a diagnostic parameter for acute cholecystitis, according to the symptom onset at the time of medical consultation (≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours), and its potential association with both medical and surgical complications.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in two urban, tertiary care emergency departments (ED) between March 2023 and June 2024. Adult patients (≥ 18 years) with clinically diagnosed acute cholecystitis were included. Presentations were categorized by time since symptom onset: early (≤ 24 hours) or late (> 24 hours). Fever was defined as axillary temperature > 37.5 °C at home or at ED arrival. The primary outcome was the sensitivity of fever for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis, stratified by early versus late presentation. Secondary outcomes included the sensitivity of other inflammatory markers and the association between fever and medical or surgical complications. The association between fever and complications was evaluated using a penalized logistic regression model (Firth method) to account for the low number of outcome events.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 207 cases of acute cholecystitis were included in the analysis: 108 early presenters; and 99 late presenters. Fever was present in 4.6% (95% CI, 1.5-10.4) of early presenters and 20.2% (95% CI, 12.8-29.4) in late presenters, with an overall sensitivity of 12.1% (95% CI, 8.0-17.2). Medical and/or surgical complications were low in this cohort (n = 15, 7.2%), but more frequent in patients with fever, regardless of time onset of symptom (28% versus 4.5%, P < .001), yielding an adjusted odds ratio of 6.64 (95% CI, 1.42-31.21; P = .02) after adjusting for leukocyte count, C-reactive protein levels, and age.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Fever is an uncommon sign of acute cholecystitis, especially in early presentations, but may indicate a higher risk for complications when present. These findings underscore the need to reconsider the role of fever in current diagnostic criteria and suggest further validation of its use as a predictor of complications in prospective studies.

articles.title: Respiratory Viral Positivity Is Associated with Decreased Risk of Serious Bacterial Infections in Febrile Infants.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Febrile infants ≤ 60 days of age are at increased risk for serious bacterial infections (SBIs), often necessitating extensive diagnostic evaluation and hospitalization. Although respiratory viral infections are common in this population and may influence the likelihood of concurrent bacterial infection, the relationship between respiratory viral panel (RVP) results and SBI risk remains an important consideration in clinical decision-making. The objective of this study was to evaluate the association between RVP results and the occurrence of SBIs among febrile infants ≤ 60 days of age.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this single-center, retrospective study we analyzed data from infants ≤ 60 days of age who presented to the emergency department with fever (temperature > 100.4 °F/38 °C) between September 2020-May 2024. Infants were divided into two subgroups based on RVP results: positive or negative for any viral infections via a multiplex polymerase chain reaction panel. The overall rate of SBI, and the rates of individual SBIs (urinary tract infection [UTI], bacteremia, and bacterial meningitis), were compared between groups. The primary outcome was the rate of SBIs among infants with any positive RVP compared to those with a negative RVP.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We analyzed 1,986 charts of febrile infants ≤ 60 days of age, of whom 485 (24.4%) met criteria. Of these, 309 (63.7%) had a positive RVP for at least one pathogen while 176 (36.3%) were all negative. Overall, the rate of serious bacterial infection in the RVP negative group was 35.8% (95% CI, 29%-43.1%) compared to 6.5% (95% CI, 4.1%-9.6%) in the RVP positive group (P < .001). Infants with a positive RVP had a significantly lower prevalence of serious bacterial infection (7.4%) and UTI (5.5%) compared to those with a negative RVP (P < .001). In the RVP positive group, 17 patients (5.5% [95% CI, 3.4%-8.5%]) had a UTI compared to 46 (26.1% [95% CI, 20.1%-33%]) in the RVP negative group. Notably, there were four cases of bacteremia (1.3% [95% CI, 0.4%-3%]) in the positive RVP group compared to 20 (11.4% [95% CI, 7.3%-16.7%]) in the negative RVP group. In the positive RVP group, there were 0 cases of meningitis (0% [95% CI, 0%-0.9%]) compared to 5 (2.8% [95% CI, 3.4%-85%]) in the RVP-negative group. The differences in bacteremia and meningitis rates between the two groups were statistically significant (P < .001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Febrile infants ≤ 60 days of age with a positive RVP are associated with a significantly lower risk for SBI compared to those with a negative RVP, a 64% relative risk reduction. If validated with a prospective study, these findings could help guide clinical decision-making, potentially allowing for a more nuanced approach to the management and disposition of febrile infants, particularly the need for invasive workup and hospitalization.

articles.title: Retrospective Comparison of the Pericapsular Nerve Group Block Versus the Fascia Iliaca Block for Hip Fractures in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Hip fractures are a common injury among the elderly and a substantial cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Pain management is an essential component of care for patients with hip fractures, particularly for improving patient outcomes. Ultrasound-guided nerve blocks such as the fascia iliaca block (FIB) are evidence-based means of providing perioperative analgesia and reducing opioid use. Newer nerve blocks, such as the pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block, may serve as alternatives to the FIB. The objective of this study was to retrospectively compare pain reduction following the PENG block and FIB in patients with hip fractures treated in our emergency department. Secondary objectives included block-related complications such as local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), greater hospital length of stay, and increase in mortality.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The primary outcome measure was to investigate whether the PENG block is an effective alternative to FIB in achieving analgesia. Secondary objectives include data on rates of LAST, block complications, hospital length of stay, and mortality. We conducted a retrospective chart review on adult patients (≥18 years) with hip fractures who received either a FIB or PENG block between June 2021 and June 2023. Among the participants, pain scores (0-10 scale) were recorded before and after the block. Opioid use 24 hours postblock was also documented. We used generalized estimating equation modeling to compare pre-to-post block pain reduction between the FIB and PENG block groups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 88 participants met inclusion criteria (73 FIB, 15 PENG). The mean (SD) preblock pain scores were 6.5 (2.1) for FIB and 7.9 (1.6) for PENG, improving to 4.4 (2.0) and 4.3 (2.1) postblock, respectively. Generalized estimating equation analysis revealed a statistically significant greater reduction in pain for the PENG group compared to FIB (mean difference = 1.42; 95% CI, 0.21-2.63; P = .02). In this study, there were no cases of local anesthetic systemic toxicity or other block-related complications observed (0%; 95% CI, 0%-3.4%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Patients who received the PENG block achieved a greater reduction in pain scores compared to the FIB in this small retrospective cohort study. These findings suggest that the PENG block may be an effective alternative to FIB for analgesia in this setting. However, larger, prospective studies are needed to confirm these results. Given the study design and baseline differences in pain scores, these findings should be interpreted with caution.

articles.title: Impact of Increasing Ambient Temperatures on Emergency Department Trauma Presentations at a Level I Trauma Center.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Global temperatures are increasing because of climate change, affecting human health. Elevated ambient temperature has been shown to increase rates of trauma presentations in emergency departments and to increase antisocial behavior, such as violent crime. To better understand how to reduce the burden on trauma hospitals, we must better understand the relationship between ambient temperature, trauma patients, and intentional injury. We sought to examine the relationship between trauma rates and minimum and maximum daily temperatures and assess whether the assault trauma mechanism had the strongest association between weather and trauma rates.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of full and partial trauma team activations that presented to a Level I trauma center in New York from 2012 to 2019, inclusive. Daily maximum and minimum temperatures were divided into quintile ranges. Traumas were classified by injury type and mechanism as either unintentional, assault, or intentional self-harm. We used generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution to examine the relationship between maximum and minimum temperature ranges and trauma rates, controlling for precipitation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Increasing daily minimum and maximum temperatures positively correlated with increasing trauma activations. While all trauma types increased with increasing temperature, assault traumas showed the highest rate of increase (P < .001). Compared to the lowest temperature quintile (< 46 °F), the two highest maximum temperature quintiles (> 73 °F and 83 °F) showed an increase in assault rates of 83% and 65% (incident rate ratio 1.83 [95% CI, 1.46-2.29] and 1.65 [95% CI, 1.32-2.07], respectively).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Trauma rates have a positive association with increasing ambient temperature rates. This temperature effect is largest among the assault group, suggesting that as temperatures continue to increase, so too will traumas that are the result of interpersonal violence.

articles.title: Low-Energy Chest Trauma in Older Adults: Prospective Study of Indications for Chest Computed Tomography.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Older adults frequently present to the emergency department (ED) with low-energy blunt chest trauma, and clinically important intrathoracic injuries may be under-detected during the initial evaluation. We aimed to evaluate whether bedside findings-particularly focal chest tenderness patterns (including anterior chest wall tenderness [ACWT] and lateral compression tenderness)-were associated with computed tomography (CT)-confirmed intrathoracic injury in older adults with low-energy blunt chest trauma, while also examining chest pain and early warning scores (EWS) as adjunct clinical variables.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A single-center prospective study included 136 patients 65 years or older presenting within 24 hours of low-energy blunt trauma that did not meet prespecified high-energy criteria. The primary outcome was any intrathoracic pathology on chest CT during the index ED visit. Secondary analyses examined associations between CT-confirmed injury and bedside findings (including chest pain, ACWT, lateral compression tenderness, thoracic spine tenderness, visible chest skin trauma, and auscultatory abnormalities), routine clinical variables, and laboratory measures; rib fracture and disposition were treated as prespecified exploratory analyses. The National Early Warning Score and Modified Early Warning Score were evaluated as exploratory physiologic comparators. Routine laboratory testing at presentation included arterial blood gas analysis. Chest CT performed during the index ED visit served as the imaging reference standard, with intravenous contrast use determined by clinical indication. The National Emergency X-Radiography Utilization Study (NEXUS) chest criteria informed routine imaging selection. Logistic regression identified independent associations, and diagnostic performance metrics were calculated for key bedside tenderness findings.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: For 136 studied patients, mean age was 78.9 (9.2) years, and 60.3% of patients were female. Ground-level falls accounted for 72.8% of injuries. Chest pain was reported in 19.9% of patients. Lateral compression tenderness (21.3%) and ACWT (25.0%) were the most common examination findings. On univariable analysis, chest pain and lateral compression tenderness were associated with intrathoracic pathology; in multivariable analysis, ACWT was the only independent bedside predictor of the primary outcome (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 4.18, 95% CI, 1.85-9.44; P < .001). For rib fracture, ACWT, chest pain, and lateral compression tenderness remained independently associated. For intrathoracic injury, ACWT had a sensitivity of 47.6% (95% CI, 32.0-63.6), specificity of 85.1% (95% CI, 76.3-91.6), positive predictive value of 58.8% (95% CI, 44.5-71.8), negative predictive value of 78.4% (95% CI, 72.9-83.1), a positive likelihood ratio of 3.2 (95% CI, 1.79-5.70), and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.62 (95% CI, 0.46-0.83), supporting its role as a rule-in bedside cue. Lateral compression tenderness was also associated with intrathoracic injury (OR 3.81, 95% CI, 1.62-8.94; P = .002).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In older adults with low-energy blunt chest trauma, focal chest tenderness findings-especially anterior chest wall tenderness, lateral compression tenderness, and chest pain-were associated with higher odds of CT-confirmed thoracic injury; however, ACWT was the only independent bedside predictor of the primary outcome. These findings function as rule-in rather than rule-out cues. Early warning scores showed limited utility for anatomic injury detection in this cohort and should not be interpreted as trauma-specific imaging decision tools.

articles.title: Computed Tomographic Appearance of Massive Intestinal Ascariasis in a Pediatric Patient.

abstract.text: Ascaris lumbricoides is among the most common intestinal helminths worldwide but is encountered less frequently in the United States. Although uncomplicated ascariasis is diagnosed clinically and by stool examination, imaging becomes important when intestinal obstruction or another complication is suspected. We report a nine-year-old boy who had recently emigrated from Guatemala and was transferred from an outside emergency department for severe abdominal pain and concern for small bowel obstruction. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an extensive burden of elongated, curvilinear intraluminal structures throughout the small bowel, several containing central gas, with associated bowel dilatation. Notably, the initial outside interpretation favored fecalized bowel contents, and the diagnosis was recognized only after the history of vomited worms prompted a radiology addendum. Stool examination confirmed A. lumbricoides ova. The child was managed conservatively with albendazole and bowel cleanout, and serial abdominal radiographs demonstrated progressive reduction in the visible worm burden without surgery. This case illustrates both the striking imaging appearance of massive intestinal ascariasis and a clinically important diagnostic pitfall in its recognition.

articles.title: Transient Gestational Hypertension and Its Subsequent Maternal and Perinatal Outcomes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe maternal and perinatal outcomes among pregnant women with transient gestational hypertension (TGH) defined through prolonged in-hospital surveillance.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort included pregnant women hospitalized at ≥20 weeks of gestation at a referral hospital in Panama between July 1, 2023, and December 31, 2024. Women were included if they had an initial systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg, with no subsequent elevated reading during seven days of measurements obtained every four hours; they were then discharged and followed until delivery. The primary outcome was the subsequent development of gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 20 pregnant women were included; mean age was 31.9 ± 6.3 years, median gestational age at the initial episode was 32.1 weeks (interquartile range (IQR), 27.9-34.2). Five patients (25.0%; 95% confidence interval, 11.2-46.9) subsequently developed a hypertensive disorder: three developed gestational hypertension and two developed preeclampsia, including one with severe features due to a hypertensive crisis. Among those who progressed, the median time to the new diagnosis was 30 days (IQR, 27-35). Delivery occurred at a median of 38 weeks; there was one preterm delivery, one neonatal intensive care unit admission, and no maternal or perinatal deaths. In exploratory analyses, progression was associated with a higher cesarean delivery rate and lower neonatal birth weight.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Even after seven days of in-hospital normotension, one in four pregnant women progressed to TGH. TGH should not be considered benign and requires subsequent surveillance, ideally with out-of-hospital blood pressure measurements.

articles.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, Practices, and Perceptions of Occupational Health and Safety Among Healthcare Workers at a Tertiary Care Teaching Hospital in Jharkhand, India: A Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.text: Background Healthcare workers encounter biological, chemical, physical, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards, yet evidence from heterogeneous hospital workforces in eastern India remains limited. This study evaluated occupational health and safety knowledge, attitudes, practices, and perceptions; quantified item-matched knowledge-practice gaps; and assessed self-reported hepatitis B vaccination uptake among healthcare workers at a tertiary care teaching hospital in Jharkhand. Materials and methods A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from April 1 to June 30, 2026. Using stratified random sampling with equal allocation, 400 participants were enrolled: 100 nurses, 100 technician/paramedical staff, 100 housekeeping staff, and 100 ward attendants. An investigator-developed bilingual 32-item questionnaire, pilot-tested among 40 healthcare workers, measured knowledge (eight Yes/No items), attitude (five items), practice (five items, including a binary hepatitis B vaccination item), and perception (four items). Domain scores were converted to percentages and categorised using prespecified cutoffs. Categorical outcomes were compared using chi-square or exact tests, and four directly matched knowledge-practice pairs were evaluated using exact McNemar tests. Results The mean knowledge, attitude, practice, and perception percentages were 64.6%, 59.9%, 55.9%, and 53.9%, respectively. Poor practice was observed in 209 participants (52.2%; 95% CI, 47.4%-57.1%), unfavourable perception in 235 (58.8%; 95% CI, 53.9%-63.5%), and an overall poor/inadequate occupational health and safety profile in 227 (56.8%; 95% CI, 51.9%-61.5%). Knowledge-practice gaps were largest for occupational injury reporting (161/400, 40.2%), followed by personal protective equipment use (151/400, 37.8%); all four paired comparisons were significant (p<0.001). Recent safety training was associated with knowledge (p=0.002) and with attitude, practice, perception, and overall category (all p<0.001). Self-reported hepatitis B vaccination uptake was 41.5% (95% CI, 36.8%-46.4%). Conclusion The findings indicate an important gap between occupational safety knowledge and consistently reported safe practice, particularly for injury reporting, personal protective equipment use, hand hygiene, and biomedical waste segregation. Competency-based training, non-punitive exposure reporting, routine workplace audits, and accessible hepatitis B vaccination should prioritise support and outsourced workers while remaining available to all occupational groups.

articles.title: Accounting for urgency: Implications of risk adjustment for surgical site infection after emergency colon surgery at safety net hospitals.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Colon operations performed for urgent indications or trauma are associated with a higher risk of surgical site infection. Prior models for surgical site infection surveillance did not account for this urgency, potentially yielding inadequate risk adjustment for surgical site infection at safety net hospitals that perform a disproportionate number of these emergency operations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We used data from the 2021 Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project State Inpatient and Emergency Department Databases from California and Florida. We evaluated index encounters during which colon surgery was performed, excluding hospitals performing <25 colon operations per year. We calculated risk- and reliability-adjusted surgical site infection rates, first adjusting for covariables modeled on the 2015 baseline National Healthcare Safety Network surgical site infection surveillance model, which did not account for trauma or emergency status: comorbidity index, diabetes, obesity, and endoscopic/laparoscopic approach; and subsequently adjusting for National Healthcare Safety Network-based covariables plus an indicator of emergency surgery. We then evaluated whether including this indicator affected the adjusted risk of surgical site infection among safety net hospitals and non-safety net hospitals.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We identified 360 hospitals that performed >25 colon operations in 2021, including 79 (22%) safety net hospitals. Safety net hospitals were more likely to be in the highest quintile of adjusted surgical site infection risk using the National Healthcare Safety Network-based covariates alone (P < .05) but not after adding the emergency surgery indicator to the model. The proportion of safety net hospitals in the highest quintile of adjusted surgical site infection risk decreased after accounting for emergency surgery.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Modifying risk adjustment models to include emergency status may reduce inadequate adjustment of surgical site infection risk after colon surgery, with important financial implications for safety net hospitals in the era of value-based incentives.

articles.title: Emergency Department-Administered Extended-Release Buprenorphine After Fentanyl Overdose Reversed by Emergency Medical Services With Naloxone.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers are on the frontline of the opioid epidemic and administered naloxone to reverse suspected overdose over 442,000 times in 2024. Interest in EMS-initiated sublingual (SL) buprenorphine (BUP) exists; however, initiation of month-long extended-release buprenorphine (XR-BUP) in the immediate postoverdose period has not yet been described. The high risk of death from repeat overdose in patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) could be reduced by administration of XR-BUP. The purpose of this case report is to highlight the utility of EMS-initiated SL-BUP followed by XR-BUP to potentially improve care linkage and adherence to medication-assisted OUD treatment.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A bystander call to 911 dispatched a Basic Life Support (BLS) unit to an unresponsive 30-year-old man found with fentanyl-smoking paraphernalia. First responders administered 8 mg of intranasal naloxone. Paramedics arrived 8 min later and assessed the patient to be in opioid withdrawal with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 22. The patient reported using heroin or fentanyl and methamphetamine daily. After consent, paramedics administered 16 mg of SL-BUP. In the ED, an addiction medicine consult service administered a 300-mg monthly XR-BUP formulation. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: We report that rapid transition from naloxone reversal of overdose and EMS initiated SL-BUP to month-long XR-BUP is possible during a single emergency medicine encounter using a stepwise clinical pathway. We hope our observations encourage further prospective study of the intervention described as this may link patients to medication assisted OUD treatment, which decreases mortality in patients with OUD.

articles.title: Ultrasound Diagnosis of Subhepatic Appendicitis.

abstract.text: Acute subhepatic appendicitis is an exceptionally rare anatomical variant (accounting for 0.01-0.09% of all appendicitis cases) that arises from embryological intestinal malrotation or incomplete cecal descent. A 39-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 48-h history of progressive right upper quadrant pain, anorexia, mild nausea, low-grade fever (37.8 °C), marked leukocytosis (19 × 109/L with a left shift), and elevated C-reactive protein (5.2 mg/L). Physical examination demonstrated localized tenderness and guarding in the right hypochondrium, with a negative clinical Murphy's sign. Bedside abdominal ultrasonography was performed utilizing a dedicated dual-probe strategy: a low-frequency convex transducer (1-5 MHz) for anatomical orientation and a high-frequency linear transducer (6-12 MHz) for targeted near-field interrogation. Graded compression identified a non-compressible, aperistaltic, blind-ending tubular structure in the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) measuring 9 mm in outer diameter with a thickened wall (3.2 mm), an appendicolith at the base, mural hyperemia on color Doppler, and surrounding hyperechoic fat stranding with localized free fluid. Real-time sonography systematically excluded acute cholecystitis, hepatic lesions, and perforated peptic ulcer. Preoperative CT was omitted, and the patient proceeded directly to emergent diagnostic laparoscopy, which confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix in the right subhepatic space adjacent to the liver margin. A laparoscopic appendectomy was successfully performed. Histopathology confirmed uncomplicated suppurative appendicitis, and the patient was discharged uneventfully on postoperative day three. Emergency high-resolution ultrasonography using a targeted dual-probe technique can conclusively diagnose subhepatic appendicitis, challenging the paradigm that CT is strictly mandatory. In patients presenting with atypical right upper quadrant pain, dedicated sonographic interrogation of the hepatorenal space facilitates prompt surgical management while eliminating ionizing radiation and diagnostic delays.

articles.title: Acute Confusion as the Presenting Feature of Hypoglycemia and Lactic Acidosis in an Adult With Known Fructose-1,6-Bisphosphatase Deficiency.

abstract.text: We report the case of a 29-year-old woman with genetically confirmed fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency, an inherited disorder of gluconeogenesis. She had been followed since childhood by a specialized metabolic unit and was brought to the emergency department by a mobile intensive care service because of acute confusion. Her symptoms had begun the previous evening with epigastric pain, repeated vomiting, anorexia, and intense asthenia. Consequently, she had eaten almost nothing for approximately 20 hours before the onset of confusion. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score recorded during the pre-hospital assessment was 8, with a capillary blood glucose concentration of 0.4 g/L (2.2 mmol/L), which was partially corrected during transfer. On arrival, her GCS score was 10. She had no focal sensorimotor deficit, and her pupils were equal and reactive. Her respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, peripheral oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg, and heart rate was 120 beats per minute. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Arterial blood gas analysis showed severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (pH 7.185; bicarbonate, 6.3 mmol/L) and a lactate concentration of 6.49 mmol/L. The full blood count showed moderate leukocytosis with neutrophil and monocyte predominance without anemia. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, performed after treatment had been initiated to exclude an intercurrent precipitating condition, was normal. She was treated with intravenous 30% dextrose, followed by a continuous intravenous dextrose infusion, and was admitted to the intensive care unit. Her consciousness returned to a GCS score of 15, and the acid-base disturbance corrected in parallel. Mechanical ventilation was not required. She was discharged from the intensive care unit after 48 hours, with complete neurological recovery. This episode did not represent a new diagnosis but rather an acute decompensation of an already known metabolic disease, precipitated by vomiting and a fast of approximately 20 hours. In a patient with a known disorder of gluconeogenesis, acute confusion following vomiting or reduced oral intake should prompt consideration of a hypoglycemic and lactic acidosis crisis until proven otherwise. Bedside glucose measurement and arterial blood gas analysis can establish the diagnosis within minutes, and intravenous dextrose is the treatment for both abnormalities.

articles.title: Vertebral artery injury in patients presenting to the emergency department with cervical spine fractures: national trends, predictors, and cerebrovascular outcomes.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Vertebral artery injury (VAI) is an uncommon but serious sequela of cervical spine trauma, with a varying reported incidence. Prior studies have been limited by small sample size and inconsistent follow-up. This study identified predictors of VAI in emergency department (ED) patients with cervical fractures and evaluated the association with ninety-day stroke.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Adult patients presenting to the ED with acute cervical fractures were identified in the 2010-2022 PearlDiver Mariner M170 database, excluding those with less than ninety days of follow-up. Demographic, clinical and nonclinical characteristics were compared between patients with and without VAI diagnosed on the same day of presentation. Multivariable regression analysis identified independent predictors of VAI. Additionally, multivariate regression assessed VAI association with ninety-day stroke, adjusting for age, sex, and Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 153,948 patients with cervical fractures, VAI was noted in 777 (0.50%), increasing from 0.33% in 2010 to 0.76% in 2022 (p < .001). Independent predictors, in decreasing OR, included upper cervical fracture (OR 1.93), high-energy trauma (OR 1.88), ECI (relative to 0: 1-2, OR 1.77; 3-4, OR 1.38), insurance (relative to Medicare: commercial, OR 1.50; Medicaid, OR 1.51), male sex (OR 1.28), and younger age (per decade decrease, OR 1.01) (p < .05 each). VAI was independently associated with stroke (OR 3.62, p < .001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: VAI detection increased over the study period, and several clinical and nonclinical factors independently predicted VAI. VAI conferred over 3-fold higher odds of ninety-day stroke. Early recognition of high-risk patients may guide strategies to reduce cerebrovascular complications.

articles.title: Drug-facilitated sexual assault (spiking) in Poland: risk perception, knowledge, and bystander intentions.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To estimate the prevalence of self-reported suspicion of spiking among adults in Poland and to examine sociodemographic determinants of suspicion, concern, symptom recognition, and preventive knowledge in the context of drug-facilitated sexual assault.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted between 18 and 27 March 2025 using computer-assisted web interviewing (CAWI). A stratified quota sample of 1,000 adults was drawn to reflect the national distribution by sex, age, and place of residence. A structured questionnaire assessed suspected exposure to a "date rape drug" (spiking), frequency of concern at social events, knowledge of intoxication symptoms, preventive knowledge, and intended bystander actions. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for associations with sex, age, education, sexual orientation, and place of residence.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Suspicion of spiking was reported by 19.4% of respondents, and 18.1% expressed frequent or constant concern. Reco-gnition of symptoms was declared by 24.4%, while 51.2% were uncertain. Preventive knowledge was affirmed by 43.8%. Intended bystander responses most commonly included contacting friends (44.0%), relatives (42.9%), venue security (41.7%), the police (38.5%), or ambulance services (36.3%); 2.5% would not intervene. Younger age was associated with higher odds of reporting suspicion (18-29 years: aOR = 3.76; 95% CI: 1.58-8.99; 30-39 years: aOR = 3.49; 95% CI: 1.44-8.46; 40-49 years: aOR = 3.30; 95% CI: 1.34-8.13; reference ≥ 60). Female sex predicted greater concern (aOR = 2.81; 95% CI: 1.91-4.15) and higher preventive knowledge (aOR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.29-2.18). Higher education was associated with better recognition of symptoms (aOR = 2.84; 95% CI: 1.10-7.36).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Suspicion of spiking is relatively common, while confidence in recognizing symptoms remains low, supporting the need for structured prevention and trauma-informed response pathways.

articles.title: Adequacy of Clinical Information in Knee Radiography Requests With Reference to the Pittsburgh Knee Rule: A Single-Centre Clinical Audit.

abstract.text: Background and objective Knee radiographs are frequently requested following acute knee injury, although the proportion demonstrating a fracture is relatively small. The Pittsburgh Knee Rule (PKR) is a validated clinical decision rule developed to support selective radiography following a fall or blunt knee trauma. Assessment of the rule, however, depends on adequate documentation of the relevant clinical findings. This clinical audit aimed to assess the adequacy of PKR-related clinical information documented on knee radiograph requests at a district general hospital with reference to the Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) AuditLive standard. Secondary objectives were to determine fracture yield and identify areas for improvement in request documentation. Materials and methods A single-centre retrospective clinical audit was undertaken. A total of 300 knee radiograph records were initially identified from two source lists. Ninety-five records were excluded during initial eligibility screening because they fell outside the predefined audit population, and three repeated or duplicate records were subsequently removed during dataset consolidation, resulting in 202 requests for analysis. The original radiology requests and corresponding imaging reports were reviewed for patient age, documented mechanism of injury, weight-bearing information, and radiographic evidence of acute fracture. The PKR was considered applicable where a fall or blunt-trauma mechanism was documented. Requests were classified as documented PKR-positive, documented PKR-negative, indeterminate because of insufficient documentation, or PKR not applicable where the documented mechanism fell outside the intended scope of the rule. Results Of 202 knee radiograph requests, 83 (41.1%) were classified as documented PKR-positive, 78 (38.6%) as indeterminate because of insufficient documentation, and 41 (20.3%) as PKR not applicable. No request contained sufficient information to establish a confidently documented PKR-negative status. Acute fractures were identified in 19/202 (9.4%) examinations. Fractures occurred in 15/83 (18.1%) documented PKR-positive requests and 4/78 (5.1%) requests with indeterminate documentation. No fractures occurred among the 41 requests classified as PKR not applicable. Conclusions A substantial proportion of knee radiograph requests lacked sufficient documented clinical information to permit reliable assessment with reference to the PKR. These findings reflect information available within radiology requests rather than confirmed real-time application of the rule by requesting clinicians. Absence of a documented criterion should not be interpreted as evidence that the corresponding clinical finding was absent or that radiography was inappropriate. An educational intervention was subsequently introduced, with a second audit cycle planned to assess improvement in documentation.

articles.title: Chronic Mercury Toxicity Associated With Habitual Dried Shark Consumption in Oman: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Mercury exposure is closely linked to the consumption of contaminated fish, particularly those containing methylmercury. Mercury toxicity presents with a wide range of nonspecific symptoms, making diagnosis challenging for clinicians. The clinical manifestations vary depending on the type of mercury, levels and duration of exposure, and individual susceptibility. We report a case of a 69-year-old woman with no significant past medical history who presented to the Emergency Department (ED) with chronic abdominal pain, muscle aches, bloating, and generalized fatigue lasting over a year. An initial evaluation in Thailand revealed an elevated blood mercury level of 38.72 μg/L during evaluation in Thailand. She was offered chelation therapy but declined and sought a second opinion in Oman. Repeated testing at the Central Public Health Laboratories two months later showed a mercury level of 24.36 μg/L (reference range <15 μg/L). Her complete blood count, renal function, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Dietary history revealed daily consumption of seafood and dried fish, including shark, as her primary protein source. Following cessation of dried fish consumption and reduction of seafood intake, blood mercury levels normalized without chelation therapy. Seafood, particularly dried fish, can be a significant source of methylmercury exposure. This case emphasizes the importance of obtaining a detailed dietary history when evaluating patients with chronic, nonspecific symptoms. Identifying dried fish as a key source of mercury exposure in Oman highlights the need for public awareness and early recognition of environmental toxic exposures.

articles.title: Condition-Linked Opioid Prescribed-Medicine Events and Subsequent Emergency Department Use Among Adults With Surgical or Procedural Events: A Longitudinal Medical Expenditure Panel Survey Study.

abstract.text: Background We examined whether an observed opioid prescribed-medicine event linked to the same condition as a surgical/procedural event in year 1 was associated with all-cause emergency department (ED) use in year 2 and whether this association differed by poverty status. These medication events represent medicines reported as purchased or otherwise obtained; the linkage does not establish postoperative timing. Materials and methods We pooled four two-year Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) panels: 2017-2018, 2018-2019, 2020-2021, and 2021-2022. Adults were eligible when a year-1 surgical/procedural event was linked to a condition record. The exposure was one or more observed year-1 opioid prescribed-medicine events linked to that same condition, compared to none. The primary outcome was the year-2 annual all-cause ED visit count, and the secondary outcome was any year-2 ED use. Survey-weighted quasi-Poisson and logistic models were adjusted for demographic characteristics, poverty, insurance, year-1 utilization, health status, surgical settings, surgical-event burden, and panel. Adjusted outcomes were standardized over the analytic population. A prespecified interaction compared people below with at or above 200% of the federal poverty level (FPL). Results Among 4,468 eligible adults, 4,454 (99.7%) were complete cases, and 816 of 4,454 (18.3%) had an observed condition-linked opioid prescribed-medicine event. Adjusted mean annual ED visits were 0.336 (95% confidence interval {CI}: 0.275-0.412) with and 0.345 (95% CI: 0.311-0.382) without a linked opioid prescribed-medicine event. The adjusted mean ratio was 0.975 (95% CI, 0.784-1.211; p=0.8165), and the mean difference was -0.009 visits (95% CI, -0.082 to 0.065; p=0.8150). Any year-2 ED use occurred in 194 of 816 exposed participants (survey-weighted, 22.5%; 95% CI, 18.9%-26.1%) and 845 of 3,638 comparators (survey-weighted, 21.5%; 95% CI, 19.7%-23.3%). The exposure-by-poverty interaction did not provide evidence of heterogeneity (ratio of ratios, 1.112; 95% CI, 0.751-1.649; F=0.284; p=0.5943). The adjusted risk difference for any ED use was -1.9 percentage points (95% CI, -5.7 to 1.8; p=0.3073). Conclusions No clear adjusted association was detected between an observed year-1 condition-linked opioid prescribed-medicine event and year-2 annual all-cause ED use. The estimates were imprecise and do not establish equivalence, the absence of an association, or socioeconomic equity. The exposure cannot be classified as postoperative because the procedure-medication sequence was not established.

articles.title: The Dangers of Chest Compression: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Chest injuries after cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) are common, but subsequent infected parasternal collections after CPR are uncommonly described. We present a case of a 49-year-old female with a history of intravenous drug use (IVDU) who developed multiple sternal and rib fractures and a large infected parasternal collection after community CPR following a heroin overdose. She was treated with antibiotics and required surgical evacuation of the collection. This case highlights the importance of recognizing and managing post-CPR chest wall complications early to prevent serious morbidity.

articles.title: Occult Incarcerated Osteochondral Fracture of the Medial Patellar Facet Following Acute Lateral Patellar Dislocation in an Adolescent: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Acute lateral patellar dislocation is a common injury in adolescents and is most frequently associated with rupture of the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL). Concomitant osteochondral fractures may remain occult or be misinterpreted on initial imaging, resulting in delayed diagnosis and potentially compromising long-term joint function. We present a rare case of an incarcerated osteochondral fracture of the medial patellar facet that was initially misinterpreted as arising from the medial femoral condyle following acute lateral patellar dislocation. A previously healthy 15-year-old boy presented to King Hussein Medical City Emergency Department approximately one week after his injury following an acute traumatic lateral patellar dislocation sustained while playing football. Clinical examination demonstrated persistent lateral patellar subluxation and knee instability. Initial plain radiographs and computed tomography demonstrated a displaced osteochondral fragment and persistent lateral patellar subluxation; however, the fragment was initially interpreted as arising from the medial femoral condyle. Although advanced imaging was performed, the anatomical origin of the incarcerated osteochondral fragment was not correctly recognized preoperatively. Surgical exploration unexpectedly revealed an incarcerated osteochondral fracture of the medial patellar facet rather than an isolated ligamentous injury. The fragment was anatomically reduced and stabilized using three headless compression screws supplemented with a suture anchor to repair the MPFL, successfully restoring the patellar articular surface and patellar stability. A structured postoperative rehabilitation program resulted in fracture healing, progressive functional recovery, and return to pre-injury activities without recurrent patellar instability. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of occult osteochondral injuries associated with acute lateral patellar dislocation in adolescents. Persistent patellar maltracking or subluxation following reduction should raise suspicion for an incarcerated osteochondral fragment, even when conventional imaging appears consistent with an isolated MPFL injury. Careful preoperative evaluation combined with meticulous intraoperative assessment is essential for identifying repairable osteochondral lesions. Early anatomical reduction and stable fixation can restore joint congruity, preserve native articular cartilage, and achieve excellent functional outcomes while potentially reducing the risk of recurrent instability and post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

articles.title: Early hemodynamic changes after the use of push-dose noradrenaline in patients presenting to the emergency department with septic shock: a descriptive study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Although continuous noradrenaline infusion (CNI) is standard vasopressor therapy during the initial resuscitation of patients with septic shock, hemodynamic stabilization may not be immediate. Push-dose noradrenaline (PDNA) has been proposed as a temporary measure while CNI is being established. However, its clinical use, dosing, early hemodynamic response, and short-term safety in the emergency department (ED) are not well described.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: To address this gap, we conducted a single-center retrospective descriptive study at a tertiary care hospital in Japan in 2019. Adults with Sepsis-3 septic shock who received PDNA in the ED and were admitted to the intensive care unit were included. We assessed the context and dosing of PDNA administration, CNI use, mean arterial pressure (MAP) within 15 min after PDNA administration, and adverse events.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 91 patients with septic shock, 50 (55%) received PDNA. PDNA was administered at CNI initiation in 25 patients, during CNI dose escalation in 6, and as rescue administration before CNI initiation in 19. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) initial PDNA dose was 20 (20-30) µg. During the 15-minute observation window, 32 (64%) patients received one bolus, 14 (28%) received two, 3 (6%) received three, and 1 (2%) received four. The directly observed median (IQR) MAP was 52 (44-61) mmHg at initial PDNA administration (n = 30) and 62 (50-68) mmHg 1 min later (n = 25). One of 36 patients evaluable for prespecified physiological adverse events experienced an adverse event; however, no serious adverse events were documented.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this single-center retrospective descriptive study, PDNA was most commonly administered at CNI initiation, and administration was followed by an early increase in median MAP. However, the noncomparative design and concurrent resuscitative interventions preclude attribution of this change solely to PDNA administration. No serious adverse events were documented; however, safety assessment was limited owing to missing data and retrospective ascertainment. These findings do not establish the effectiveness or safety of PDNA. Prospective comparative studies with standardized monitoring are required.

articles.title: A Hidden Catastrophe: Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Presenting as Acute Ischemic Stroke.

abstract.text: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening emergency that typically presents with hypotension or abdominal pain but rarely with primary neurological deficits. We report the case of a 74-year-old woman presenting with acute focal neurological deficits concerning for ischemic stroke, whose preceding abdominal pain and lower extremity mottling ultimately pointed toward an alternative diagnosis. Point-of-care ultrasound and subsequent computed tomography angiography revealed a ruptured infrarenal AAA. We discuss how consideration of these additional clinical features led to the correct diagnosis and prevented inappropriate thrombolytic therapy. Given the time-sensitive nature of stroke management, this case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis and considering aortic pathology in patients presenting with acute neurological symptoms.

articles.title: Thirty-Day Outcomes in Ultrasound Versus CT-Only Imaging in Obese Adults With Acute Appendicitis.

abstract.text: Background Acute appendicitis is one of the most common surgical emergencies affecting people worldwide. Current guidelines suggest imaging with an immediate computed tomography (CT) scan as the gold standard imaging pathway. However, emerging research has suggested that the addition of an ultrasound (US) can play a role in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis. In this study, we wanted to see if US as an adjunct to the existing imaging pathway of a CT scan had any improvement in 30-day outcomes in adult obese patients. Method Using data gathered from real patients using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study on adult obese patients (BMI ≥ 30) with acute appendicitis who were diagnosed by US, with or without a CT scan, versus those who received only a CT scan. In order to balance for possible confounding variables, propensity score matching (1:1) was used to match for common demographic information and comorbidities known to worsen surgical outcomes (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, BMI). The study's primary outcome was emergency room revisit rate after their initial visit. Secondary outcomes included peritoneal abscess, perforation, and peritonitis. All outcomes were measured at 30 days after the acute appendicitis diagnosis. Results After propensity score matching, 968 patients were deemed eligible for analysis, with 484 patients within each cohort. There were no detectable statistical differences between these groups after matching for patient demographics and comorbidities. Those who underwent a US did not show significant differences in outcomes compared to those who received a CT scan only. The rates of emergency room revisits were similar between the US and CT scan groups, at 11.98% and 13.64%, respectively (RR = 0.879, p = 0.44). For secondary outcomes, no statistical difference was found for the risk of peritoneal/abdominal abscess (RR = 0.69, p = 0.16), perforation (RR = 1.32, p = 0.35), or peritonitis (RR = 0.90, p = 0.59). Conclusion Our study demonstrated no statistically significant difference in outcomes for adult obese patients diagnosed with acute appendicitis who received an ultrasound, compared to those who received a CT scan only.

articles.title: From Heart Murmur to Bone Involvement: Tricuspid Valve Endocarditis With First-Rib Osteomyelitis in a Patient With Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) Bacteremia.

abstract.text: Tricuspid valve infective endocarditis (TVIE) is most commonly associated with intravenous drug use and Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. While right-sided endocarditis may present with septic pulmonary emboli, hematogenous spread to the bone is a rare but serious complication. Among osseous sites, first-rib osteomyelitis is particularly uncommon and may be underrecognized in patients presenting with localized chest pain or swelling.
